stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: A hydrogen atom sits in front of you. Its electron can only occupy the discrete levels $E_n = -13.6 / n^2$ eV drawn on the left. Send in photons of energy $h\nu$ (right slider) from different starting states $n_i$ (left slider). Watch which photons are absorbed and which pass through.
stages.concept: Bohr quantization: bound-state energies form a discrete ladder $E_n = -\dfrac{E_1}{n^2}$ with $E_1 = 13.6$ eV. Absorption is allowed only when the photon's energy matches an exact level gap: $h\nu = E_{n_f} - E_{n_i} = E_1 \left(\dfrac{1}{n_i^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_f^2}\right)$.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: A target transition is highlighted on the diagram: bring the atom from the marked $n_i$ up to the marked $n_f$. Set the starting level and tune $h\nu$ until the arrow tip lands on the target line.
stages.concept: For a chosen initial state $n_i$ and a chosen final state $n_f$, exactly one photon energy works: $h\nu^{*} = E_1 \left(\dfrac{1}{n_i^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_f^2}\right)$. Any other value passes through — the spectrum is a line spectrum, not a continuum.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: The energy-level diagram is hidden. You are told the initial state $n_i$ and the target final state $n_f$ only. Compute $h\nu$ on paper from the Bohr formula, then set the two sliders to your answer and submit.
stages.concept: Rearrange for the photon energy: $h\nu = E_1 \left(\dfrac{1}{n_i^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_f^2}\right)$ with $E_1 = 13.6$ eV. One shot per attempt — a wrong submit rotates to a different transition.

labels.tip1: sweep both sliders — try many n_i and many h-nu, notice only certain values absorb
labels.tip2: match the target: set n_i to the marked level, tune h-nu until the arrow tip hits n_f
labels.tip3: compute h-nu on paper first, then set both sliders and submit once
labels.peek_tip_formula: h-nu = 13.6 (1/n_i^2 - 1/n_f^2). Substitute the target n_i and n_f, in eV.
labels.peek_tip_anchor: Balmer (n_i=2) transitions are in visible range 1.9-3.4 eV; Lyman (n_i=1) are UV, 10-13 eV.

1.1: Not every h-nu produces absorption. Try holding n_i fixed and slowly sweeping h-nu — most values pass through.
1.2: When absorption happens, the arrow tip lands exactly on another level. What is the algebraic condition? h-nu equals a specific level-to-level gap.
1.3: For n_i = 2, the smallest absorption is n=2 to n=3 at h-nu = 13.6 (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.89 eV. Try it.

2.1: Read the two dashed levels on the diagram: one is your n_i, the other is n_f. Set the n_i slider first.
2.2: Only one photon energy climbs from n_i to n_f. It is h-nu = 13.6 (1/n_i^2 - 1/n_f^2). Plug in and set the slider.
2.3: If the target says n_i = 2 and n_f = 4: h-nu = 13.6 (1/4 - 1/16) = 13.6 x 3/16 = 2.55 eV.

3.1: The diagram is gone but the formula E_n = -13.6/n^2 is not. Write out E_i and E_f for the given n_i and n_f.
3.2: Then h-nu = E_f - E_i = 13.6 (1/n_i^2 - 1/n_f^2). Compute the two reciprocals, subtract, multiply by 13.6.
3.3: Do not forget to set n_i on the discrete slider before submitting. Both n_i and h-nu must match.
